channel.title: EverythingTech
channel.description: A daily tech newspaper. 45+ sources, read in full and edited by an LLM every morning.

item.title: Cursor Marketplace's Claude Code extension shipped an SSH backdoor in versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313
item.description:
The compromised builds ran with the editor's permissions, so any machine that installed them should be treated as exposed until checked.

Security firm Phorion found a persistent SSH backdoor inside the official Claude Code extension for VS Code as distributed through the Cursor Marketplace. Cursor has removed versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313. The original advisory named only the later build, but Cursor's updated notice on 31 October added the earlier one for macOS and Windows. Extensions run with the permissions of the editor and the user, so once the module loads it can read local files, source code and developer tools without asking for anything else.

On macOS the implant tries to turn on Remote Login and then drops SSH keys and a persistence mechanism. Phorion found a bug in the first step. When run as a standard user, the command used to check Remote Login prints an administrator-access error and exits successfully rather than reporting that the service is off. The script only enables SSH when it reads "Off", so on a Mac that had no SSH running, the inbound access path never gets switched on. The keys and persistence still get written, which means a machine can be compromised even though the remote door stays closed. One headline in our sources puts the exposure window at nearly twelve hours.

item.title: Binance hack grows to $6.3 billion, with most of it drained in about 20 minutes
item.description:
Our October 30 coverage put the loss near $2 billion; tracing firms now put it at about three times that and say most of it moved in one short window.

This updates our October 30 story, which put the loss near $2 billion. Tracing firms now put the theft at about $6.3 billion from Binance wallets across at least ten blockchains, including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana. TRM Labs says most of it left in roughly 20 minutes on October 29, and that one attacker sent the funds to multiple addresses. Binance has suspended deposits and withdrawals while it investigates, and says it and other firms have frozen about half of the stolen funds so far.

The attack was prepared well ahead of time. According to TRM, the operator tested early code on two wallets, then ran a dress rehearsal on a third and sent that test money back to its own address. Roughly four hours later, that code was running on a Binance hot wallet, and the drain followed. Elliptic's chief scientist says North Korea is likely responsible, and TRM says the tactics resemble those of a group known as TraderTraitor. If that attribution holds, the theft would nearly double everything North Korea has stolen in crypto so far. The open question is how much of the rest can be frozen, since much of it may already be out of reach.

item.title: Open-weight model GLM 5.3 turned unreleased Firefox security fixes into working browser exploits
item.description:
Researchers estimate about $1,000 per Firefox version, using only information that was public when each release shipped.

Researchers found that GLM 5.3, an open-weight model released by Z.ai in August, could read security fixes that were published but not yet in a Firefox release, then build an exploit from them. The proof of concept was a webpage that, when a Firefox user visited it, read a file from the visitor's computer and sent it to the attacker with no further clicks. Under their setup, any Firefox release from September 17 through October 26 could be compromised this way.

Researchers call the stretch between a published fix and the moment users receive it the patch gap. Until now, using that window took serious time and skill, or access to the most capable cyber-focused models. The authors say their setup was meant to mimic a relatively unsophisticated attacker, and that once it was running each Firefox version cost about $1,000 to attack. In the successful cases the model also used an undisclosed vulnerability alongside the patch-gap ones. Mozilla shipped Firefox 159.0 on October 27 with a fix for that undisclosed bug. The authors say this should make the attacks harder, but they do not claim it closes the gap.

The problem is not specific to browsers. Any project where a model can read upcoming security changes before release is exposed, and open-source projects are the most exposed because their code is public. The authors expect the threat to grow as open-weight cyber capabilities improve.

item.title: Deno's team joins Cloudflare and the Deno runtime stops development within a year
item.description:
That leaves three server-side JavaScript runtimes, and the author argues the browser market's history suggests one of them will end up dominating.

Deno's whole team is joining Cloudflare, and development of the Deno runtime will end after one year. Ryan Dahl, who created Node.js and started Deno in 2018, made the announcement. That leaves the server-side JavaScript market with Node.js under the OpenJS Foundation, Bun, which is now owned by Anthropic, and Cloudflare's workerd. Workerd is built mainly for Cloudflare's own Workers platform, so only two of the three are general-purpose runtimes.

The author's case rests on history. After Internet Explorer 6 had roughly nine in ten browser users, Microsoft largely stopped working on it, and developers spent about five years writing for one browser's quirks. Competition from Firefox, Safari and Chrome eventually restored progress, but the browser market then consolidated again, with nearly every browser now built on one of three engines. On the server side, Node stagnated under its sponsor until contributors forked it as io.js in 2014, and the two projects reunited under a neutral foundation in 2015. Dahl started Deno to add features he considered critical, including first-class TypeScript and promise-based APIs throughout, so those ideas now depend on what the other runtimes choose to adopt.

What is still open is whether anyone forks Deno during the one-year window, and whether its design choices survive in Node or Bun. The piece does not name a fork or a successor project.

item.title: Five new flaws in Azure API Connections let one tenant take over other tenants' Key Vault and SQL connections
item.description:
The researcher says the same design weakness keeps resurfacing across Azure Logic Apps connectors, and the five bugs in this set paid about $200,000.

A researcher reports five more vulnerabilities in Azure API Connections, the component that connects Azure Logic Apps to external services. Each one gives an attacker the same primitive: the ability to make Microsoft's shared API Management layer act on a connection the attacker does not own, and so use the victim's stored token against the victim's backend. The author says the reach is broad, covering cross-tenant access to Key Vaults and Azure SQL databases, and any other connected service such as Jira or Salesforce. The author says the bugs netted about $200,000 in total.

The architecture explains why. A logic app calls the shared API Management instance, which checks the action against the connector's OpenAPI definition, exchanges the caller's key for the backend token configured on the connection, and makes the call. In the author's account, each bug lets the attacker reach the token that the exchange step attaches to someone else's connection. The author argues that input validation is the only thing standing in the way, and that the edge cases are hard to close in every system at once. The author's earlier posts in this series described the same architecture and an earlier cross-tenant compromise.

The excerpt we have does not describe what Microsoft has changed or when the fixes shipped. The author says a talk at BlueHat Asia 2026 covers the findings, with a recording to follow.

item.title: Northflank breach leads users to rotate secrets after unauthorised use of their AI API keys
item.description:
Northflank says its investigation is still open, and it is telling every customer to assume their environment variables were decrypted.

Northflank, a developer hosting platform, disclosed a breach on October 30 and told every customer to treat their environment variables as compromised. Users reported that AI API keys stored on the platform were being used without their permission. Northflank has enabled audit logs for all customers, including free accounts, and has turned on secret rotation for Postgres and MongoDB addons.

The company's guidance is to rotate every user-supplied secret, including those in workloads, secret groups and global secrets. It also says to revoke each old key with its provider and to disable public access on any addon where it is turned on. Northflank has not confirmed what was taken or how the access happened, and its investigation was ongoing at the last update in our text. The indicators it shares overlap with addresses in Wiz's "Black October" report, which describes attacks aimed at AI credentials.

Stolen AI keys are attractive because they can be used at scale and billed to the victim. The provider's usage and billing logs are the fastest way to see whether a key was abused.

item.title: bunny.net wiped a compromised CDN node in Armenia and reissued its platform TLS certificates
item.description:
The company found no evidence the node or its data was accessed, but it cannot rule out that possibility, so it reissued certificates as a precaution.

bunny.net says an infrastructure provider reported unauthorized access involving third-party server management software. One of its CDN nodes, in Armenia, ran on a server from that provider. The company stopped routing traffic through the server within 20 minutes, preserved security logs, wiped the machine, revoked its access to other systems and removed the server from its infrastructure.

Neither bunny.net nor the provider has found evidence that the node or its data was accessed, though the provider's investigation continues. If the node was reached, bunny.net says the data at risk would be content cached there for a short time, pull zone settings and the TLS certificates kept on that machine. It has revoked and reissued all certificates for its own platform domains, and said reissuance for custom domains would finish within 24 hours of the notice. No account data was on the server, according to the company.

Customers on managed certificates need to do nothing. Customers who manage their own certificates should revoke and reissue them with new private keys, as bunny.net recommends.

item.title: Applebee's app shipped a hardcoded database password that exposed customer personal data, now fixed
item.description:
A researcher used AI to find the credential in the Android app's source, and it gave access to names, contact details, birth dates and login IP addresses.

Applebee's has fixed a flaw that let anyone read personal information about registered customers. The restaurant chain's Android app, popular enough to pass a million installs on Google Play, contained a password for an internal customer database. Researcher Robert Wiggins used AI to find it in thousands of lines of code. TechCrunch decompiled the app to confirm the credential was there, then created an account with dummy data and used the credential to retrieve it from the database.

The exposed records included names, email addresses and whether each address was verified, dates of birth, phone numbers and ZIP codes. They also held veteran status, login counts, account creation dates and the IP address of the most recent login, which can reveal approximate location. Wiggins said the credential would also have let an attacker change customer data.

Wiggins could not report the problem directly, because neither Applebee's nor its parent Dine Brands had a way to receive security reports. He asked TechCrunch to help, and the outlet held its story until the fix was confirmed. The article does not say how long the credential was in the app.

item.title: OpenAI will honour a shared robots.txt signal for AI training preferences, and other labs are reportedly following
item.description:
The OpenAI post's details are not in our text; this account rests on its standfirst and a summary of a report that other major labs are adopting the same signal.

This story is written from the headline and standfirst of OpenAI's post, plus a summary of a report from The Verge. The full text of either was not available to us, so the mechanics of the signal are not covered here. According to the standfirst, OpenAI will honour a shared robots.txt signal that lets website operators state their AI training preferences to participating providers. The Verge's summary says Google, Microsoft and Anthropic plan to adopt the same standard, which would give publishers one place to state an opt-out for several large labs.

The appeal is that a site states its preference once, instead of keeping a separate rule for each company's crawler. The standfirst does not say how providers verify the signal, or what happens to content they have already collected.

item.title: DoorDash cut its AI grocery reorder from 16 seconds to 2 by precomputing recurring purchases
item.description:
The change doubled shopping list views and lifted the reorder flow's order rate by about 34 percent, according to DoorDash.

DoorDash's grocery reorder flow in Ask DoorDash used to rebuild a shopping list with an agent on each request, which took about 16 seconds. The team moved that work offline. Batch LLM inference now identifies likely recurring purchases from 90 days of history and consumer profile signals, and deterministic checks validate the output before the lists are stored. At request time, the system just reads the stored list and resolves each item against the current catalog, so latency fell to about 2 seconds.

The serving path tries the original store item first, then a catalog product identifier, then a search term. That lets the system handle changed listings and unavailable products without asking the model to reason about them again. DoorDash credits the change with doubling shopping list views and raising the flow's order rate by roughly 34 percent. The company's shared agent platform supplies orchestration, memory, tracing, evaluation and rollout controls, and domain teams own their instructions, tools and evaluation criteria. DoorDash says adding its Reservations agent took one week, about ten times faster than its first domain agents. The article does not say how quickly precomputed lists go stale, which is the main open question for this design.

item.title: Netflix's GPU platform keeps training jobs running by draining and replacing unhealthy nodes automatically
item.description:
Netflix reports GPU-node availability above 99.95 percent, and says job success rose from about 98 percent to more than 99.5 percent.

Netflix has described a reliability platform for large GPU training and inference, built on Kubernetes. A training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs in lockstep, so one failed GPU, a degraded network adapter or a slow machine can stall the whole job. Netflix says its approach has lifted GPU-node availability above 99.95 percent, and job success from roughly 98 percent to above 99.5 percent.

The key finding is that a cloud health check only shows that a VM is running, not that its GPUs can do distributed training. Netflix found GPUs that answered status queries but failed once memory was allocated or sustained computation began. It also found network adapters that were present but had fewer links than expected, which let collective operations continue at a fraction of their bandwidth. Device checks use NVIDIA's DCGM tooling, network checks count and inspect the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces, and a node agent turns the results into Kubernetes node conditions that controllers act on.

The checks fail closed, so a hung diagnostic marks the machine unhealthy, and kernel logs serve as a fallback when the GPU diagnostics themselves break. Remediation escalates: a transient problem blocks new work, a persistent one drains the node and moves its workloads, and the actions range from killing a job or resetting a GPU to rebooting or replacing the machine.

item.title: Microsoft retires Azure Deployment Environments in February 2027 and names no replacement product
item.description:
Teams are told to write Bicep or ARM templates directly, which means rebuilding the provisioning but not the self-service catalog the product offered.

Microsoft will retire Azure Deployment Environments on February 22, 2027, and its retirement guide lists no successor product. Microsoft Dev Box goes on September 18, 2028, and Microsoft points customers to Windows 365 instead, saying plainly that it is not a like-for-like replacement. Teams have about sixteen months to move.

The guide's alternatives are direct infrastructure-as-code deployment with Bicep or ARM templates, reusable Azure verified modules for governed building blocks, and CI/CD pipelines for provisioning. On third-party tools it is blunter: none of the ones it reviewed support a Bicep or ARM lifecycle. Microsoft gives no reason for the retirement.

The product's real value was a governed catalog of pre-approved templates, role rules and a developer-facing portal, which platform engineers used to publish standard environments. Bicep and pipelines can reproduce the provisioning, but not that catalog or portal, and that territory now belongs to tools such as Backstage, Port and Humanitec. An engineer quoted by InfoQ says the product's advantages were hard to replicate with Bicep, Terraform or Pulumi, and that the API was unstable and the documentation sparse.

item.title: Anthropic drops the five-hour Claude Code limit for verified Ultra subscribers, while weekly caps stay
item.description:
Max 5x becomes Max and Max 20x becomes Ultra, at the same $100 and $200 monthly prices, and current subscribers need to do nothing.

Anthropic has removed the rolling five-hour usage cap for Claude Code users on its top plan, provided their accounts are verified and they still have weekly usage left. The change came alongside a rename: Max 5x is now Max, and Max 20x is now Ultra, at the same monthly prices. The five-hour cap could halt a developer partway through a debugging session or a large refactor even with weekly allowance left, so its removal matters most to people running long agent sessions.

Not every Ultra subscriber gets the change immediately. Anthropic says verification happens automatically from account and payment history, that users cannot request it or speed it up, and that it will email people once the cap is lifted. The weekly limit still applies. The pricing page lists Ultra at 10 times Pro's weekly usage, against 5 times on Max, and chats count toward the same weekly limit as Claude Code on web, desktop and mobile. Once that allowance runs out, usage credits keep work going at standard API rates, billed on top of the subscription.

item.title: Meta moves Just-in-Time Tests into production to catch bugs in code changes before they land
item.description:
Meta reports that the tests let engineers find more bugs while easing load and producing fewer spurious failures.

Meta's Catching Just-in-Time Tests, or JiTTests, are no longer a research prototype and now run as part of its infrastructure. The system uses LLMs to generate tests for each code change, and those tests are designed to fail when the change introduces a concrete behavioral difference. That surfaces bugs in diffs before they reach production. Meta says the approach helps its engineers catch more bugs, with less load and fewer false positives.

The method differs from LLM code review. A review model reasons about a diff the way a human reviewer would, while a JiTTest produces executable evidence of the change in behavior. Meta says that takes more computation, but it catches classes of bugs that review-style tools can miss. The hard part at a codebase of hundreds of millions of lines is separating strong catches, which are real bugs, from weak catches that are probably false positives. Meta's paper, "Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta", covers the initial deployment in detail. The excerpt we have does not include the precision or coverage numbers.

item.title: Factory's Droid 1.0 agent harness runs hundreds of tool calls inside a single model request
item.description:
Factory says Droid is up to 20 percent more efficient than the native harnesses built for each model on the same tasks, a result the company measured itself.

Factory has released Droid 1.0, an agent harness that covers the prompts, tools, tool-result handling and loop around a model. The headline feature is a programmatic tool-calling engine that lets a model run hundreds of tool calls in one request, which Factory says suits models that plan whole workflows as code. The company claims Droid beats the harnesses that model vendors build for their own models, on efficiency, by up to 20 percent on the same tasks.

Factory is model-independent, and offers an auto router, Factory Router, that picks the model or mix of models for each task. Its improvements come from an internal Agent Factory, where agents study benchmark failures and friction from real user sessions, propose harness changes and test each change on every model family it affects. Engineers review the evidence before anything ships. The excerpt we have does not name the benchmarks or the task counts, so the 20 percent figure is a vendor measurement and not an independent one.

item.title: Spawn reports 77,000 shipped changes in 30 days from a ten-person team spending $3.1 million on tokens
item.description:
Spawn's founder says the company spends about 30 times its payroll on AI tokens, and that its agents now ship changes at a pace close to Anthropic's own output.

Spawn is a ten-person company that ships to players, and its founder says it runs what they call a fleet: permanent AI agents, each with a name, a memory of past work, real permissions in company systems and ownership of an area such as the engine, finance, operations, bug triage or deploys. In the last 30 days the fleet shipped 77,000 substantial changes, about 108 an hour, and the company spent $3.1 million on tokens. The founder says the team now ships about 500 times what it did six months earlier, and that the setup only began working once Anthropic released its Fable models.

These agents are long-lived, unlike the short Claude Code sessions most people run for a single task. Each one spins up helper swarms for its work, and on most days the fleet creates thousands of them. The five humans on the team also use a modified Claude Code for bigger projects that need closer steering. The founder argues the difference is the operating model, with a small human team supervising a large agent team, rather than a large human team that uses AI tools.

All of these figures are self-reported. The article does not explain how a "substantial" change is counted or how quality is tracked, so the throughput numbers cannot be compared directly with a team that counts differently.

item.title: PostgreSQL 19 slips past its usual autumn release as AI-generated bug reports overload maintainers
item.description:
The release is now expected in November at the earliest, and the lead developer blames a flood of AI-driven reports and back-branch security work.

PostgreSQL 19 will miss its usual September-to-October release window and is now expected in November at the earliest, possibly later. Robert Haas, a PostgreSQL developer, has blamed AI-driven load for the delay. The project is seeing a surge of bug reports from AI and LLM agents, and it also has to backport security and bug fixes to older supported versions.

Haas says the volume of bugs means more fixes overall, and that LLM-drafted fixes are not always correct or compliant with PostgreSQL's standards. Human committers still have to review and commit each one, and their capacity has not grown with the report volume. Time that would have gone into reviewing the release went into security issues and back-branch bugs instead. That in turn slowed the decisions about which changes to revert before version 19 shipped, and he links the late reverts directly to the slip.

For users, the timing is the main takeaway. The article gives no firm date beyond "at least November" and does not say what share of the reports were AI-generated.

item.title: Salesforce agrees to buy defense logistics startup Rune for $375 million
item.description:
Rune's AI helps the U.S. military predict supply needs and manage field logistics, and Salesforce plans to plug its frontline data into its Missionforce defense unit.

Salesforce is buying Rune Technologies in a $375 million cash-and-stock deal, per Resilience Media. Rune makes AI tools that let the U.S. military forecast supply requirements and coordinate logistics in the field. Salesforce did not respond to a request for comment.

The deal extends Salesforce's Missionforce defense unit from back-office planning into battlefield operations, by bringing Rune's frontline logistics data into the platform. Salesforce says its Missionforce defense unit has grown 80 percent since launching last year, partly on a 10-year Army contract worth $5.6 billion. Rune was founded in 2024 and has raised about $30 million, including from Andreessen Horowitz, Point72 Ventures and In-Q-Tel. Its last valuation was $127 million, in a Series A, which makes the price roughly three times that mark. The purchase also adds to a busy year of Salesforce deals, including its agreement to buy the AI agent platform Fin for $3.6 billion.

item.title: Blackstone now expects Anthropic to get a high junk rating after its IPO
item.description:
Blackstone had previously expected an investment-grade rating before 2027, and now expects the top tier of speculative grade instead.

According to a Financial Times report relayed by TechCrunch, Blackstone expects Anthropic to receive a high junk rating after its initial public offering. Blackstone is the anchor investor in a $63 billion deal to finance Anthropic's chips. It previously told investors the company would receive an investment-grade rating before 2027. It now expects double-B, the highest tier of speculative grade, which is a reversal. Anthropic and Blackstone both declined to comment.

The forecast is a prediction, not a rating decision, but the stakes are clear. A junk rating would make it harder and more expensive for Anthropic to borrow to fund the large compute deals it has signed over the past year, a spending pattern that has worried investors. Anthropic filed to go public earlier this week, and the actual agency ratings will show whether Blackstone's view is shared.

item.title: Google's TPU-equipped satellite returns its first answer from orbit, a haiku from Gemma 4
item.description:
The on-board Gemma 4 model wrote a haiku about space after Google booted the satellite's TPUs, the first test of the Project Suncatcher hardware in orbit.

Google's Project Suncatcher satellite, launched earlier this month, has produced its first response from space. Google booted up the satellite's Tensor Processing Units, and the on-board Gemma 4 model followed a prompt to write a haiku about being in space. Google also says it tried space-themed limericks and telemetry prompts. Project Suncatcher is an experiment that could eventually place AI data centers in orbit.

The next tests will check how the TPUs hold up under thermal stress and radiation exposure in orbit. Google plans a pair of interconnected satellites in 2027, which it calls the next milestone toward workloads that run reliably in space. The demonstration shows one satellite booting its accelerators and answering prompts. It does not report throughput, power or latency, so it confirms that the hardware works in orbit rather than that it has any capacity to spare.

item.title: curl's config files were Turing-complete for nine months, until 8.17.0 added an include cap
item.description:
The reduction assumes unbounded strings and steps, and the real binary has neither, so it is not Turing-complete in practice.

Between curl 8.12 and 8.16, a config file could cut variable values into pieces and pull in other config files, with nothing bounding how deep that went. Put together, those features let a researcher build a simulator for any two-counter Minsky machine. With unbounded strings and resources, that construction counts as Turing-complete, and curl 8.17.0 broke it with a five-level include cap.

The construction is concrete. A counter is a string of repeated characters, each instruction is a config file whose name acts as a label, and a special expansion selects the next file to run. The author shows four files that add 2 and 3. The real binary limits expansion to 10 million bytes and bounds recursion through the C stack. On 8.12, a bare countdown loop managed only 922 steps on an 8 MB stack before it crashed with a segfault. The cap's pull request frames it as protection against a config file that includes itself indefinitely, and its regression test runs that very case and expects an error. The public explanation does not mention Turing completeness or explain why five was chosen.

item.title: Alasdair Allan says AI coding claims were overstated, and the career ladder for juniors is losing rungs
item.description:
Allan argues the more important question is what software engineering looks like when engineers no longer have to write the code themselves.

In a conference talk, Alasdair Allan revisits Dario Amodei's claim from a year earlier that AI would write essentially all code within 12 months. Allan cites a Redwood Research analysis that puts the figure nearer 50 percent when only code committed to repositories is counted, with the 90 percent number relying on throwaway scripts and transient text. Google reports just over 25 percent of its internal code is AI-generated, and Microsoft reports about 30 percent. Allan also cites Anthropic internal data showing engineers use Claude for about 59 percent of their daily work, and Claude Code authoring roughly 4 percent of GitHub commits.

Allan's main claim is that writing code was never the core of the profession, so the debate about AI-written code misses the question of how engineers develop. He draws on METR and Anthropic research to describe a "supervision paradox": junior engineers who rely on AI tools lose the practice that builds judgment, while teams still need reviewers who understand the code. The excerpt we have ends before the talk lays out its proposed progression model, so this piece covers the argument's premise, not its remedy.

item.title: Ollie, a privacy-focused AI assistant, shuts down on November 6
item.description:
CEO Bill Lennon says the company got close but could not keep up, and that rivals made it harder to stand out and raise money.

Ollie, an AI assistant built around user privacy, will shut down on November 6, its CEO Bill Lennon said on X. Ollie connected to a user's email and calendar and offered bookings, meal planning and bill payments for families, on a subscription. Customers will get instructions for exporting their data and for refunds in the coming days.

Ollie raised a $7.5 million seed round led by Khosla Ventures and was one of the first mainstream apps to earn SOC 2, an independent audit of security and privacy controls. Lennon said the company got close but could not keep up. He named rival assistants, including Muse and Instinct, as making it harder to stand out and to raise the capital it needed. The article also notes that privacy has rarely been a profitable differentiator in tech, and that many new assistants raise privacy problems of their own.

item.title: AWS's James Ward argues MCP servers should tell agents what to do next, not just return data
item.description:
AWS's workaround for the missing trace IDs in MCP is a session ID parameter on every tool, so a team can follow an agent's full path.

James Ward, a principal developer advocate at AWS who sits on the technical committee of the Agentic AI Foundation, argues that many MCP servers are just thin APIs: the agent asks for data and gets it back. He wants tool responses to include guidance on what the agent just did, what it might do next and where to find more. He describes MCP as another voice in the conversation, rather than a database.

Ward also raises visibility. MCP has no built-in trace ID, so AWS adds a session ID parameter to its tools and tells agents to pass it on every call. A second parameter carries the user's prompt or a summary of their goal. Teams can then stitch calls into one journey, compare what the user wanted with the path the agent took, and build evaluations from the gaps. Ward also said AWS ships a CLI and skills alongside MCP, partly because MCP's OAuth model cannot switch between AWS profiles the way the CLI can.

item.title: Fujifilm will spend about $63 million to expand LTO tape output fivefold by fiscal 2028
item.description:
Fujifilm credits generative AI's data growth for the demand, and it points to offline tape as a defense against ransomware.

Fujifilm will invest about 10 billion yen, roughly $63 million, to raise its magnetic tape production capacity fivefold, measured against fiscal 2025 levels. The work runs from fiscal 2026 through 2028, at the Odawara site of its Kanagawa Factory, and is mainly for its latest LTO Ultrium 10 tape. Fujifilm calls it the largest investment it has made in dedicated LTO tape facilities.

The company ties the demand to generative AI, which it says is driving exponential growth in the data that needs archiving. Cloud and data center operators already use tape because it stores large volumes at low cost, and a tape cartridge that is disconnected acts as an air gap against ransomware. The announcement is a supply signal rather than a demand figure, since it gives no volumes, customers or prices.

item.title: Reddit will require login to browse, ending two decades of logged-out access
item.description:
CEO Steve Huffman says curbing unauthorized scraping and automated traffic is a key reason, and that he has concluded the change is right.

This story is written from a Slashdot summary, the only text available to us, so the start date and any details for third-party apps and researchers are not covered here. According to the summary, Reddit plans to require users to log in before they can browse posts and discussions, ending the practice of allowing logged-out visitors. CEO Steve Huffman says the decision is meant in part to curb unauthorized scraping and automated traffic. He calls it a big change for him personally, given how much his life has been shaped by the open internet, and says he has concluded it is the right decision.
